acceptedReports.program: Heat resilience, local cooling and climate policy

what: Climate Resolve works on local climate policy, neighborhood cooling and technical assistance in Los Angeles.
It supports indoor-heat protections and installs cool roofs with partners in neighborhoods including Pacoima, Watts and Wilmington.
Its broader work includes transportation, wildfire resilience, planning and international cool-surface initiatives.
strengths: Cool roofs and effective indoor cooling offer a plausible way to reduce heat exposure in vulnerable neighborhoods, and the organization reports specific installations.
Implementation work could help tenants obtain useful protection beyond an adopted rule, while local partnerships connect policy with projects.
The current local projects and complete recipient accounts make additional funding, exposure and household costs concrete questions for donors.
reservations: Additional compliance, occupied cooling exposure, utility gains and marginal gift responsiveness remain unmeasured judgments.
Energy bills, rent, landlord capital, displacement and roof savings can offset health benefits; household incidence and donor room are unknown.
The estimate prices a partial local cooling pathway; broader organizational and nonlocal effects remain unestimated.

sections.what:
Climate Resolve (EIN 46-4736278) combines policy, implementation, technical assistance and community engagement. Its [2025 year-end account](https://climateresolve.org/winds-of-change/) reports more than 40 cool roofs in Pacoima, Watts and Wilmington and local public-space cooling projects. These named places are within LA County. [Shine On](https://climateresolve.org/shine-on-initiative/) also works internationally, whose global climate benefits cannot simply be assigned to LA residents.

The original FY 2025 return describes heat standards, county plans, resilience funding, wildfire recovery and neighborhood work. An ordinary gift supports that recipient, not an assumed restricted roof project. The donation route was verified without making a transaction. [Original FY 2025 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/464736278/202620709349301592/full)
sections.monitoring:
An [original county report dated July 14, 2025](https://file.lacounty.gov/SDSInter/bos/bc/1188278_EstablishingaSafeMaximumTemperatureThresholdforResidentialUnitsDirective1Jan23.2024Item47.14.pdf) supplies a 97,124-unit unincorporated rental inventory in Table 1. It is an estimated inventory, not homes needing cooling. The same report says retrofit needs cannot be quantified from assessor data and notes enforcement, grid and tenant-cost concerns. Its countywide 75% air-conditioning survey is not an observed fraction for those rental units.

A [randomized crossover experiment](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38329752/) exposed 16 older adults to four eight-hour indoor temperatures. It found greater core-temperature and cardiovascular strain at 31°C and 36°C, with much less change at 26°C. This establishes physiological plausibility, not a QALY effect or mortality rate for an 82°F ordinance. The [Pacoima field study](https://doi.org/10.1088/2515-7620/ad2a8e) concerns thermal conditions around reflective pavement, not randomized clinical outcomes; surface-temperature reductions are not equivalent to residents' whole-day exposure reductions.

Monitor effective cooling during occupied heat-hours, electricity affordability and actual use, resident symptoms and utility, complaint resolution, landlord compliance and displacement. Compare supported buildings with otherwise-similar buildings already receiving county or utility help. For roofs, verify replacement timing, preexisting code/rebate obligations, occupancy, exposure change and coating durability.
sections.qualitative:
The county rule applies to unincorporated rentals. Enforcement starts in January 2027, with small-landlord room exceptions and possible extensions. Existing rebates, public assistance and landlord obligations belong in the baseline. The city's amended motion does not establish a final citywide ordinance, so no citywide rental cohort is priced.

The physiological crossover study supports heat-strain plausibility but does not measure the model's clinical utility weights. Roof and solar projections, or pavement surface changes, cannot establish occupied personal exposure or causal household savings. The reported $300,000 savings projection mixes installations without a verified horizon or breakdown and is not assigned to annual roof savings. Additional jobs and broader climate or resilience effects remain unmeasured.
sections.cost:
The conditional central is **$22.87 million per better life**, meaning ten combined healthy-year equivalents. A $10,000 normalization yields 0.00708457 clinical QALYs and −0.00271146 consumption-equivalent years, totaling 0.00437311. The initial $14.12 million health-only illustration is preserved and reproduces when financial effects are excluded. The change follows signed resource assumptions, not measured clinical deterioration.

The denominator is the full gross annual recipient expense of $3,745,093, including support, fundraising and events once. One year's organizational work is assumed to improve additional implementation beyond existing funding and accelerate protection for three years before the baseline catches up; roofs receive five finite years. The first benefit occurs one year after an October 2026 gift. There is no perpetual law benefit or retrospective purchase of laws or installed roofs.

Clinical inputs retain the initial assumptions: 97,124 inventory units, 25% with meaningful unmet cooling need, 2.5 residents per unit, a ten-point additional coalition implementation effect, 10% recipient causal share and 50% funding responsiveness. Each effective resident receives 20 equivalent relieved days at a utility gain of 0.05. The roof illustration uses 40 units, 50% additionality, three residents, 20 days and utility 0.02. These are priors. More than 40 reported installations in 2025 do not verify a future annual cohort or unrestricted donor queue.

The financial ledger counts households rather than every resident. Unincorporated tenants have a judged $30,000 resource baseline and $100 annual net productivity gain after taxes, benefits and work costs. A positive overlap adjustment halves this to $50. Full annual costs of $120 for energy, $60 for rent and $20 for user participation are jointly deducted before logarithmic valuation, leaving −$150.

Separate landlord households are assumed to own two units each, live locally and have a $60,000 baseline. Per unit, the $60 rent transfer is offset by $120 in annual net capital-service or financing costs from accelerated implementation and $10 maintenance: −$70 per unit, or −$140 per owner. These incidence and residency assumptions are unverified. The $120 is a provisional acceleration opportunity/service cost, not a full retrofit purchase repeatedly charged. An upfront stress replaces it with a one-time $1,000 per unit cost, jointly netted in the first year, yielding $38.06 million per better life. A separate case adds one-time counterfactual expenditure relief when the baseline catches up at year four, yielding $20.05 million. Neither amount is an observed cost or refund.

Owner-occupied roof homes in incorporated Pacoima, Watts and Wilmington are geographically separate from the unincorporated policy cohort. Judged annual bill savings of $150 are halved for positive overlap, then full recurring maintenance and operating user costs of $40 are deducted, leaving $35 on a $30,000 baseline. The $40 is not a repeated upfront payment. These figures do not come from the solar savings projection. A separate utility/counterparty ledger judges $20 of net margin or displacement loss per roof across ten owner units with a $60,000 baseline, half local. It does not treat all electricity revenue as profit. All negative costs remain full.

The production income method nets each household's dollars before the logarithm and counts resource equivalents once; clinical QALYs stay separate. [Comparison method](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/cost-effectiveness/) Clinical-null and failed-thermal cases retain the entire negative financial ledger and have no beneficial price. No additional installation gives true zero unless a gift induces participation costs, which can persist after failure. Unknown incidence retains a health diagnostic with no combined price. Adverse rent, energy or capital costs can outweigh health gains. Other sensitivities test owner concentration, overlap, delay, duration, baseline resources, clinical effects and funding; they are scenarios, not confidence bounds.

Public and partner capital, enforcement, nonlocal counterparty burdens and broader portfolio effects remain unpriced. Donor expense and household welfare losses are distinct; the same capital must not be added twice. This is a partial local comparison, not complete world welfare, a full societal ratio, a lower bound or a donor-ready recommendation.

The counterparty ledger prices the illustrative utility margin loss from roof savings. Additional tenant electricity payments could also create utility margin gains; their net household incidence is unknown and unpriced here, rather than established as zero. A complete resource ledger would net policy-energy gains and roof losses for overlapping utility households in each year before logarithmic valuation. This partial central therefore cannot be described as total household resources or complete world benefit.
sections.funding:
Fresh original returns for FY 2023–2025 reconcile gross expenses of $3,311,328, $3,626,028 and $3,745,093, averaging $3,560,816.33: Part IX plus separately netted event costs once. Latest Part IX expense is $3,582,432 and event costs $162,661. Programs were $2,538,921, management $663,918 and fundraising $379,593 before event costs. Net assets of $906,954 include $603,069 restricted and $303,885 unrestricted. The return indicates an independent audit; its actual opinion and control findings were not obtained. These dated figures do not identify a current priced marginal funding gap.

Request current unrestricted staff and contract allocations, additional compliant buildings beyond the 2027 baseline, roof replacement timing, partner finance, a costed donor tranche and monitoring of household bills, capital costs and displacement. Existing rebates, county enforcement and developer or utility-funded installations remain alternatives. No restricted best-program donation or fundraising outreach is implied.

Roof user 40 means recurring maintenance/operating user cost, not a repeated upfront payment. Assumed-local landlord residency/disjointness remain unverified; nonlocal owner/counterparty effects are unpriced.
model.uncertainty: Conditional planning reference retains initial health and adds explicit signed-resource priors. None of household baselines/dollars, unmet need, marginal compliance or QALY utilities is measured by sources. Complete organizational welfare remains unknown; not a lower bound or calibrated expected value. Policy electricity-counterparty gains are unknown and unpriced; modeled roof margin losses do not constitute complete total-resource incidence.

historicalAlphaModel.costScope: Entire recipient annual gross resource expense: Part IX plus separately netted event costs. This is not restricted to Shine On. Additional public and landlord capital is excluded from the donor price but included in a disclosed sensitivity. The numerical estimate covers the heat component, not the full portfolio.
historicalAlphaModel.geographicAttribution: g=1 for modeled unincorporated LA County rental units and named City of LA roofs. County rule not applied automatically to incorporated cities or Orange County. Global Shine On effects unpriced.
historicalAlphaModel.formula: Q_LA(D) = (D / C) × [U × f × h × p × a × b × (H × u / 365) × A3 + R × z × hr × (Hr × ur / 365) × A5], where AT = sum from t = 1 to T of (1.03)^(-t). U = 97124; f = 0.25; h = 2.5; p = 0.1; a = 0.1; b = 0.5; H = 20; u = 0.05; R = 40; z = 0.5; hr = 3; Hr = 20; ur = 0.02; C = 3745093. Price per ten QALYs = 10 × D / Q_LA(D). Q_total = Q_heat + Q_other - Harm; the other-portfolio and harm terms remain unknown.
historicalAlphaModel.counterfactual: Existing county law, inspectors, utility help, landlord obligations, existing code-compliant roof replacement, partners and other advocates continue. Only additional implementation/acceleration and genuinely additional roofs credited; no retroactive policy win.
historicalAlphaModel.attribution: p is coalition-level additional effective compliance; a is Climate Resolve causal share; b is ordinary funding responsiveness. Roof z combines replacement and partner/funding additionality. Incorporated roof sites separated from unincorporated policy denominator. No media-view, carbon-offset or public-grant multiplier.
historicalAlphaModel.uncertainty: Subjective heat-component central, not calibrated posterior or full portfolio. Physiological and thermal evidence supports mechanism, not QALY weights. Native scope and current cost are observed; most conversion/attribution factors are priors. Finite 3-year acceleration and 5-year roof benefit; zero/downside retained.
historicalAlphaModel.nativeOutcomes: Additional effectively cooled resident-years and equivalent symptom/stress-relieved days in LA/Orange boundary; not cool roofs, grants, laws, workshop attendance or ambient surface degrees themselves.
